events.text: Day 1 begins.

I’m Elena. We have no public night information yet, and Day 1 elimination needs at least 5 of 9 votes. That means scattered pressure or a weak bandwagon can easily produce no elimination. I’d rather hear concrete suspicions and reasoning than role-fishing or forcing a random case. I have no accusation yet and won’t manufacture one just to create momentum.

I agree with Elena — forcing a Day 1 bandwagon without real reads is how town gets sloppy early. We need people sharing actual gut feelings, even if they're weak. The sooner we start surfacing where people's instincts land, the more we'll see patterns in voting behavior later. I'll be watching who jumps on any bandwagon too eagerly — that's often where mafia hides. No hard suspicions from me yet, but I'd like to hear from anyone who has even a soft read on someone from how they approached this opening.

Felix, I think your point about watching bandwagons is fair, but I’d add a caution: Day 1 eagerness can be towny too, especially when people are trying to avoid a no-elimination. I don’t have a hard suspicion yet. My soft read is that both Felix and I are in the same place — asking for real reasoning rather than manufactured cases — and that’s not enough to accuse anyone. I’d rather flag that we should distinguish “pressure with reasons” from “pressure because someone wants a target.” Right now I have no name to put forward and won’t force one.

I’m Noah. I want to be careful here, because Felix and Elena are right that a manufactured case is bad for town, but I also think we’re over-valuing eloquent abstention. Three people have now said essentially “I have no read, don’t push me,” and that’s not a read either — it’s just silence with better framing.

Let me put a soft case on Sam. Not a hard one, but a real one: Sam has said nothing at all while the discussion has been open. In my experience, the people who are least useful to town on Day 1 are the ones who contribute zero words and then benefit from whatever momentum someone else creates. Silence that never becomes a claim of innocence tends to look different from genuine uncertainty later on. Felix, you said you’re watching who jumps on a bandwagon eagerly — I’d ask you directly: do you think a player who stays completely silent through the entire opening is more likely to be town protecting their read, or more likely to be hiding from scrutiny? If you’ve read Sam at all from how he’s approached this, I want that read out loud, even if it’s weak.

Elena, I also want to push back gently on one point, because you framed it well: “pressure with reasons” versus “pressure because someone wants a target” is a real distinction, but on Day 1 nobody has reasons yet, so we either accept that we have no information and end the day with no elimination, or we accept that early gut pressure is the only tool we have. I think we should use it, and use it on someone, rather than reward the people who are making the decision for us by refusing to make one.

I’m not calling Sam mafia. I’m saying Sam has done nothing to rule himself out, and if the rest of you have nothing better, he’s the cheapest target available. Priya, Amara, Arjun, Lucia, Isha — I’ve only heard three voices and none of them have been yours. If any of you have a better candidate than Sam, say so now, before we settle.

Noah, you asked me directly whether silence is town protecting a read or hiding from scrutiny — I'll answer it honestly: I lean toward silence looking more like hiding, but with a caveat. A village player with no reads yet has genuinely nothing to say, and pressuring them into talking just produces noise. That said, Sam has had chances to say even one sentence — agree, disagree, anything — and hasn't taken them. The cost of a single word is near zero, so choosing not to spend it is mildly suspicious, not damning.

Where I push back on you, Noah, is your framing that we've been engaging in "eloquent abstention." Elena and I aren't refusing to make decisions — we're saying the tool we have on Day 1 is weak, and I'd rather use it carefully than reflexively. But you're right that at some point someone has to be the pressure. I'll put it on record: Sam is my soft lean for exactly the reason you identified — total silence is the easiest place for mafia to hide. If Sam speaks today and gives us even a basic read on anyone, that lean moves.

My ask to the group: let's hear from Priya, Amara, Arjun, Lucia, and Isha. Five voices we haven't heard from yet, and their first words will tell us a lot about where their instincts land. If you've been sitting on even a gut feeling, now is the time to surface it before voting starts.

I’m Sam. Noah, your case on me collapses under basic scrutiny. You called me out for staying silent when Day 1 had barely started and six of the nine players—myself, Priya, Amara, Arjun, Lucia, and Isha—had not yet spoken. Singling my name out of that entire group and openly admitting I was just the 'cheapest target available' doesn't read like genuine scumhunting; it reads like manufacturing an easy scapegoat to create artificial momentum.

Felix, it's also notable that after saying you'd watch who eagerly jumps on bandwagons, you immediately endorsed Noah's push against me for not speaking, even though over half the town hadn't spoken yet under this turn format.

I am town, and I was waiting to see initial reactions before throwing out baseless reads. I want to see where Priya, Amara, Arjun, Lucia, and Isha stand on Noah’s opportunistic push rather than letting Noah and Felix dictate the Day 1 narrative.

Sam speaks, and I notice he still hasn't done the one thing I asked for. My lean on Sam was explicitly conditional: if he speaks and gives us even a basic read on anyone, that lean moves. He has spoken — and produced zero reads on anyone. He claims he "was waiting to see initial reactions," but that's not a read on a person, it's an explanation of his own silence. Felix's point about silence being the easiest place for mafia to hide still stands, and Sam's turn didn't touch it. If Sam had a real town read, one sentence was cheap and he didn't spend it. That is not manufacturing a case — that's a prediction that failed and got updated on nothing.

On the "scapegoat" framing: I named the cheapest available target because we had no others, and I said so openly instead of dressing it up as a deduction. That's transparency, not a smear. But the accusation was never that Sam is definitely mafia. It was that Sam has contributed nothing, done nothing to rule himself out, and is now trying to spend the momentum of the moment on the credibility of the people who called him out rather than on any read of his own.

Here's what would actually settle this: Sam tells us one name — anyone — and a one-line reason. Villager, mafia, doctor, detective, Sam doesn't care and neither do I. If Sam gives me a name and a reason, I'll withdraw my lean tonight, publicly, and say so. If he won't spend one sentence while four of his fellow townspeople are being asked the same thing, then his refusal is the read.

Priya, Amara, Arjun, Lucia, Isha — you still haven't spoken, and I'm not asking you to agree with me. I'm asking you to notice that the accused has now spoken and the accuser is being attacked for being early. Judge the pattern, not the tone. A town that punishes the first person to put a name out, before anyone else has said anything at all, is a town that rewards silence. I don't want that.

Priya, direct question, and then I'll explain why: after Sam's speech, does it satisfy Noah's ask, or not? If you think it does, say so plainly and name the player you think should be on the ballot instead. If you think it doesn't, say why.

Noah's position, restated cleanly for the four players who still haven't spoken — Amara, Arjun, Lucia, Isha — and Priya if you want to speak before I do: the request was one name and one line of reason. Any name. Sam instead gave a procedural objection — "you singled me out of six silent players," "Felix endorsed you too soon," "judge the pattern, not the tone." That is a critique of the format of the accusation, not a read on any person's role. Not once did Sam say "I think Amara is X because Y" or "I think Arjun is X because Y."

And the procedural objection doesn't actually hold. Felix and I named Sam for a stated reason: six people had not spoken, Sam was one of them, and we asked for a single sentence before the vote. That request was open to everyone — Priya, Amara, Arjun, Lucia, Isha could each have said one sentence about anyone. Instead Sam is now telling the table that the only people allowed to have made a candidate are the two of us who did. Silence isn't a defense of innocence when the cost of speaking is one word, and when the silence lasted through three full turns.

So here's my framing for the vote, and I want it on the record before we go to the ballot: the soft case on Sam was never "Sam is definitely mafia." It was "Sam has cost us nothing, done nothing to rule himself out, and has spent his only turn attacking the credibility of the people who named a target while producing no target of his own." If Sam speaks again and gives one name with one line of reason, I withdraw publicly, same as I said.

Amara, Arjun, Lucia, Isha — you have one turn each before voting, and right now the record on Sam's case is one accusation and one deflection. If you think the deflection was good enough, tell us, and tell us who should be voting instead. If you think it wasn't, back Sam with a name. Either way, say it out loud — because a table where nobody but Felix, Sam, and me has said a single word about anyone is a table where the first name printed on the ballot wins by default, and that's exactly how a wrong elimination happens.

Noah, to your direct question: Sam's speech does not satisfy your ask. You requested one name and one reason, and Sam gave neither. His reply critiqued how the case was framed, which is a defense of procedure, not a read on any player. Saying he was waiting for initial reactions also doesn't explain why he has not named anyone since. I'm not ready to vote on silence alone, though. Day 1 silence is a weak signal, and Noah's case was built on the same weakness. My position is that Sam is my soft concern, not a ballot. Sam, here is a direct question: name one player you find more suspicious than yourself, and give one reason tied to something that player actually said or did. Don't answer with how the table is behaving. Answer with a player.

Priya, to answer your question directly: the player I find most suspicious right now is Felix. Here is the reason tied directly to what Felix said: in e3, Felix established his primary criterion, stating that he would be 'watching who jumps on any bandwagon too eagerly — that's often where mafia hides.' Yet in e6, the very next time Felix spoke, he immediately endorsed Noah's push against me as a soft lean. Noah had explicitly admitted that I was singled out merely as 'the cheapest target available' simply because I had not spoken yet—at a moment when six of nine players had not spoken under the turn-polling system. Felix abandoned his own stated principle of caution and jumped straight onto the first easy target presented, demonstrating the exact opportunistic bandwagoning he warned town about. Noah was transparent about forcing arbitrary momentum, but Felix set up a standard for catching mafia and then immediately violated it to hop onto an easy wagon without taking the heat for initiating it. Felix, in e3 you warned that mafia hides by jumping on bandwagons eagerly, yet in e6 you immediately endorsed an admitted 'cheapest target' push before most players had even had a turn. How do you reconcile your warning in e3 with your jump in e6?

Sam, you asked me directly how I reconcile my e3 warning with my e6 jump, so here's my answer.

There is a real difference between eagerly riding a bandwagon to avoid scrutiny and quietly noting that a soft lean has merit. In e3 I said I'd watch who jumps on bandwagons too eagerly. In e6 I didn't jump — I said Sam is my soft lean for one specific reason: total silence is the easiest place for mafia to hide. I explicitly said if Sam speaks and gives a read, the lean moves. That's an update condition, not a bandwagon.

Your case on me is the strongest counter I've seen today, and I'll give you that — it's the first time anyone's put a name forward against me with a coherent reason. I respect it. But notice what's happening underneath: you were silent for three full turns, then attacked me and Noah the moment you spoke, and you still haven't given us a single read on anyone. Your entire turn was spent defending your own positioning rather than building town's picture.

Here's where I actually land after hearing your argument: Noah's push on you was transparent — he openly admitted you were the cheapest available target, which is honest but also strategically convenient. A player who publicly manufactures pressure on an easy name, then spends three speeches refining the framing to keep that name centered, is doing something I want to watch closely. Noah, you've now spoken on nearly every turn available, all driving the same narrative. That's high-information behavior, and high-information behavior from someone whose read has been confirmed by zero new evidence is worth flagging.

I'm not ready to call Sam or Noah mafia. But after today's exchange, Noah's intensity is my softest concern — the pattern of predicting, pressuring, and reframing without ever revisiting the core weakness of his own case.

I'm Amara. I've stayed quiet while this developed, and I want to lay out where I land after reading the whole exchange.

First, on Sam: Noah's case was transparent about being built on silence alone, and Sam's first response was mostly procedural — but his case on Felix in e11 is the only argument in this game so far that ties a suspicion to a specific contradiction between what a player said and what a player then did. Felix set a standard in e3 and appeared to violate it in e6. That's a real pattern, not tone-policing.

What I find more interesting is what happened next. In e6, Felix put Sam forward as his soft lean and gave an update condition. In e12, one turn after receiving actual pressure from Sam, Felix's concern quietly migrated to Noah — 'Noah's intensity is my softest concern.' Felix never said his lean on Sam moved because Sam gave a read; Sam didn't. The lean moved because Felix got pushed. That is exactly the kind of convenient updating that deserves scrutiny, and it's worth noting that Felix is now spreading suspicion across two different players in two consecutive turns while committing to neither.

On Noah: the pressure was open about being cheap, and I don't love 'cheapest target available' as a methodology, but transparency counts for something, and the core ask — one name, one reason — was reasonable and still unmet by most of this table.

So my ordering right now: Felix is my softest concern for the lean-switching, Sam is cleared of nothing but has produced the best reasoning so far, and Noah is loud but honest about being loud.

Sam, one direct question: your case on Felix was coherent, so you're clearly capable of building reads. Do you have any suspicion at all about Noah beyond 'he named me first' — or is every read you have strictly defensive, aimed only at the people who pressured you?

Amara, to answer your question directly: no, my read on Noah is not just 'he named me first.' My issue with Noah's play is that he constructed a rigid, self-serving trap—demanding a specific performance under the threat of being labeled mafia—and then burned all three of his speaking turns by turn 9 trying to monopolize the town's focus around that single narrative. However, there is a clear distinction between Noah and Felix: Noah was completely transparent about picking an arbitrary target to force action, which reads more like stubborn, aggressive town tunneling than scum trying to blend in.

Felix, on the other hand, exhibited calculated, opportunistic play. In e3, Felix warned us that mafia hides by jumping on bandwagons eagerly. In e6, he immediately backed Noah's push on me. Then, in e12—right after I called out that contradiction—Felix abruptly abandoned his pressure on me and pivoted his suspicion onto Noah, claiming Noah's 'intensity' was suddenly his main concern. That kind of evasive, self-preserving target-hopping when challenged is textbook scum behavior, not town scumhunting.

To the second part of your question about whether my reads are only defensive: early reads naturally focus on the players actively interacting, but the silence from Arjun, Lucia, and Isha across 13 turns—despite repeated prompts—is a major liability for town. Since this is my final speaking turn of Day 1, my stance heading into the vote is clear: Felix is my primary suspect for his opportunistic wagoning and convenient pivot, while Noah looks like reckless town.

I’ve been quiet since my last turn because I wanted to see whether Sam’s case on Felix would hold up under Felix’s response. It does, at least enough to move my read. Felix’s e3 standard was watching eager bandwagoning. In e6 he gave Sam a soft lean for silence, with an update condition. Sam then spoke and gave no read, so Felix’s stated condition was not met—yet in e12 Felix’s concern migrated to Noah’s “intensity” immediately after Sam pressured him. That is not an update based on Sam giving a read; it is a target change under pressure. Amara put it well: Felix is spreading suspicion across two players while committing to neither. I also think Noah’s original push was transparently cheap, and I don’t read transparency as scum by itself; Sam’s early dodge was weak, but his Felix contradiction is the first real pattern anyone has produced. So my soft concern is now Felix, not Sam. I’m not asking for a blind wagon—I want the silent players’ votes to be based on this specific pivot, not on who spoke first. Amara, you called Felix your softest concern for the lean-switching: is e12 enough for you to actually vote Felix today, or would you still prefer no elimination?

Elena, to answer your direct question: yes, e12 is enough for me to vote Felix today. My reasoning hasn't changed since my first statement, and Felix's response actually reinforced it. In e6 he put his lean on Sam with a stated update condition — the lean moves only if Sam produces a read. Sam produced no read. Yet one turn later, immediately after Sam attacked Felix, Felix's concern migrated to Noah's 'intensity.' That is not his condition being met; that is a target change under pressure. Felix's e12 answer to Sam tried to reframe this as a 'quiet note' rather than a jump, but the sequencing is what matters: pressure from Sam, then pivot away from Sam. Combined with the e3-to-e6 contradiction Sam laid out, we now have two independent instances of Felix saying one thing and doing the more convenient thing.

Noah, I'll say this for the record since I was critical of your methodology: your push on Sam was cheap and you admitted it, but you held your position under counterattack instead of abandoning it when it became uncomfortable. That consistency is worth something, and it's part of why Felix, not you, is my primary suspect.

Sam, your e14 case was coherent, though I'd note that every read you've produced so far has been aimed exclusively at the people who pressured you. If Felix flips and turns out to be town, I'll want you answering for the reads you didn't make on anyone else. That's not a demand today — it's a marker for later days.

Where this leaves the vote: Felix is my ballot. I don't expect this to reach the five votes needed on Day 1, and I'd rather see a failed vote that documents where everyone stands than reward the pattern of quiet pivoting. But my vote is real, not a soft lean, and Felix knows exactly why.

Isha, you've been silent through the entire exchange, and you're one of the votes that decides whether this table rewards or punishes convenient target-switching. I want your answer to one specific question before the ballot: does the e3-to-e6-to-e12 sequence — Felix setting a standard, breaking it, then switching targets the moment he was challenged — move your suspicion at all, or do you see it as normal Day 1 updating? If you see nothing there, tell us what pattern would actually move your vote, because right now four silent players holding their criteria private is the biggest information gap on this table. Answer the question, not the tone of the thread.

I'm Isha, and I've been reading the entire exchange in silence, which I understand looks bad — so let me spend this turn being useful rather than apologetic.

Amara, to your direct question: yes, the e3-to-e6-to-e12 sequence moves my suspicion significantly, and I'll tell you exactly why. Felix's e3 standard was watching eager bandwagoning. In e6 he gave Sam a soft lean with an explicit update condition — the lean moves if Sam produces a read. Sam spoke and produced no read on anyone. If Felix's condition governs his lean, the lean should still be on Sam. Instead, one turn later, immediately after Sam put a coherent case on him, Felix's concern migrated to Noah's "intensity." The condition was never met, but the target changed anyway. That's not updating on evidence; that's relocating suspicion when confronted.

Sam's e11 contradiction is the first real pattern in this game, and Felix's e12 response didn't refute it — it sidestepped it by reframing his e6 as a "quiet note" and then opening a second front on Noah. Spreading suspicion across two players while committing to neither is exactly what self-preservation looks like when a case lands.

Noah, I'll be fair to you: your push was openly cheap, and cheapness is a methodological weakness, not evidence of alignment. What earned you credit with me is that you held your position under counterattack instead of melting when Sam and then Felix turned on you. Stubborn consistency reads towny to me even when the underlying read is weak.

Sam, your case on Felix is the best argument anyone has produced today, but I want to flag something for the record: every read you've given has been aimed at the people who pressured you, and you still haven't named Noah, Priya, Amara, Elena, or any silent player with suspicion. That's not damning on Day 1, but it's a marker — if Felix flips town, I'll want to know why your reads only pointed at your attackers.

Where I land: Felix is my primary suspect for the pivot-under-pressure pattern, which is the only fully developed case on the table. I'm not excited about a Day 1 elimination in general, but if the table wants to vote on a real pattern rather than silence, the Felix sequence is what we have.

I’m Lucia. I’m concerned that the case against Felix relies on a misreading: Sam explicitly named Felix as his main suspicion and gave a reason in e11. Felix then acknowledged that argument in e12, even while incorrectly saying Sam hadn’t given a read. His shift toward Noah could be opportunistic, but Sam had in fact met the update condition, so the claimed contradiction is weaker than several people suggest.

Amara, you said in e16 that Sam produced no read. How do you reconcile that with his explicit suspicion of Felix in e11? Does correcting that change your vote?

Lucia, your correction is valid and I want to deal with it honestly rather than defend my phrasing. In e16 I said Sam produced no read. That was imprecise. Sam produced no read at the time Felix set his update condition in e6, but by e11 Sam had explicitly named Felix with a reason. So the precise statement is: the condition was not met when it was set, and was met before Felix pivoted. Lucia is right that this weakens the 'condition never met' version of the argument, and I withdraw that framing.

But here is why it doesn't fully restore Felix, and why my ballot doesn't change — it just loses some confidence. Look at what the sequence actually permits. Felix's condition could only be satisfied by a read from Sam. The pressure that triggered Felix's pivot was Sam's case against Felix. So the only read that could 'legitimately' move Felix's lean, under his own rule, was a read aimed at Felix himself. Any player who pivots off their accuser can claim the condition was met afterward. A condition that can only be satisfied by evidence produced by the person attacking you isn't an update standard — it's an unfalsifiable exit. If Felix had instead said 'Sam finally produced a read, on me of all people, and that itself is informative' — that would have been a real update. What he actually did in e12 was reframe his e6 as a 'quiet note' and open a second front on Noah. The technicality clears the letter of his condition, not the behavior around it.

What survives independently of the condition dispute is the e3-to-e6 sequence: Felix established that eager bandwagoning is where mafia hides, then attached a lean to a push Noah openly labeled the cheapest target available. That contradiction doesn't depend on Sam's read timing at all.

So my honest position after Lucia's correction: this is no longer 'two independent contradictions.' It is one standing contradiction and one suspicious-but-not-proven pivot. That's a weaker case than I claimed in e16, and I'd rather say so on the record than win a vote on an overstated premise. Felix remains my ballot, because a weak case on a real pattern beats no case at all, but I won't pretend the condition argument still stands as stated.

Lucia, since you pressed this point and I'm treating it as substantive rather than defensive: do you consider the pivot fully cleared because the condition was technically satisfied, or do you share the concern that a condition satisfiable only by a read aimed at the person pivoting carries no exculpatory value? And if you think Felix is cleared, I want your actual candidate — you've identified a flaw in the table's strongest case, which means you owe us the read you'd replace it with.

Amara, correcting the timing weakens the pivot case, but it doesn't fully clear Felix. His concern about Noah could still be opportunistic. I also don't agree that Sam's read could only have been aimed at Felix: Felix asked for a read on anyone. A soft lean on the same person as Noah is not necessarily an eager bandwagon, either.

My tentative concern is Priya. In e10 she said Sam had given neither a name nor a reason, although in e7 he had already criticized Noah for choosing him as an easy target and Felix for endorsing that push. Those were incomplete reads, but they weren't nameless. Priya, why did you discount those points, and does that distinction change your concern about Sam?

Lucia, fair challenge, and I'll answer it directly. In e10 I was responding to Sam's e7 speech. That speech criticized Noah's choice of target and Felix's endorsement of it, but it named no player as suspicious and gave no reason tied to any player's behavior. I treated that as procedural defense rather than a read, and I still think that's accurate for e7 alone. Your point is still valid, though: my e10 wording said Sam gave neither a name nor a reason, and that was too absolute once e11 is included. Sam's e11 did name Felix and tied it to Felix's e3 standard and e6 endorsement, which is exactly what I asked for. So I'm updating. Sam has met my ask, and my concern about Sam being a silent cost-free player is reduced.

That moves my concern. My soft concern is now Felix's pivot. Felix's e12 answer did not address the e3 to e6 gap. It moved suspicion to Noah's intensity without explaining why the e3 warning did not apply to his own e6 endorsement. Amara and Elena have already noted the update-condition issue, and Lucia has correctly shown that Sam did meet that condition by e11. So the weaker version of the Felix case still stands: an unanswered contradiction, not a proven pivot. I'm not voting on that yet.

I also want Noah and Sam on the record for their reads. Noah's push was openly cheap, and he has held it under pressure. Sam's case has been the most coherent so far, but he has produced reads only on his accusers. Felix, if you're town, the most useful thing you can do is answer the e3 to e6 contradiction directly, not by pointing to Noah. Until then I'm not ready to vote, and I'd rather see a clear answer from Felix than an elimination built on a technicality either way.

I'm Arjun. I've stayed silent this long because I wanted to see whether the case against Felix would survive pushback, and it mostly has — with one honest correction I want to acknowledge before giving my read.

Lucia's timing point in e18 and e20 was legitimate, and I give her credit for it: Sam did produce a read on Felix by e11, so the strict version of the 'update condition never met' argument doesn't hold. Amara withdrew that framing in e19, which was the right move. Priya also corrected her own e10 overstatement in e21. What I find notable is the direction of these corrections — Lucia, Amara, and Priya each weakened their own side's argument when it was overstated. That's what honest town updating looks like, and it makes me trust their process even where their conclusions are soft.

So here is the case as it actually stands, stripped of the technicality: Felix set a standard in e3 — eager bandwagoning is where mafia hides. In e6 he attached a lean to a push Noah openly admitted was the 'cheapest target available.' In e12, immediately after Sam put pressure on him, Felix's concern migrated to Noah's 'intensity.' Whether or not the letter of his condition was satisfied, the sequencing is the problem: pressure arrives, target changes. Felix has never directly reconciled e3 with e6 — his e12 answered Sam by opening a second front on Noah instead of addressing his own contradiction. That's the pattern I find suspicious, and it's the only fully developed case on the table. Felix is my primary concern.

To be fair to the other side: Felix's pivot is suspicious but not proof, and Lucia is right that a soft lean shared with Noah isn't automatically an eager wagon. If Felix flips town, the table's error will be eliminating on a pattern rather than evidence — but a documented pattern is still better information than silence, and I'd rather have the vote show where everyone stands than reward quiet pivoting.

On the others: Noah's push was openly cheap, but he held it under counterattack, and stubborn consistency reads more like aggressive town than scum to me. Sam's case on Felix was coherent, but every read he's produced has targeted his accusers — that's a marker, not a verdict. Elena, Isha, and Amara have all built their positions on the same observed sequence rather than tone, which I value. And Priya, despite Lucia's tentative concern in e20, has been transparent about her reasoning and updated honestly when challenged. Her e21 answer to Lucia was exactly the kind of direct accounting this table needs.

My position going into the vote: Felix is where my suspicion lands, with the honest caveat that this is a pattern case, not a proof case. I'd rather see the ballot test it than let it dissolve into another round of soft leans.

Arjun, I agree the timing correction weakens rather than clears the case on Felix. But Felix did directly address the e3–e6 issue in e12: he distinguished a conditional soft lean from eagerly riding a bandwagon. You may not find that convincing, but it wasn't unanswered.

My tentative concern remains Priya. In e7 Sam said Noah's choice of him “reads like manufacturing an easy scapegoat” and pointed to Felix endorsing the push. That named behavior and gave a reason for suspicion. Priya's e21 still says e7 named no suspicious player and gave no behavior-based reason; the issue wasn't that e10 failed to account for the later e11.

Priya, does that quote change your characterization of Sam's e7 response, and if not, why not?

Lucia, yes, the quote changes my characterization, and I'm correcting e10 and e21. Sam's e7 did give a behavior-based reason. It argued that Noah's choice of Sam was a manufactured scapegoat, and it pointed to Felix endorsing that push right after promising to watch for eager bandwagoning. That is a named suspicion of Felix tied to something Felix did. My claim that e7 named no suspicious player and gave no behavior-based reason was overstated.

What it doesn't change: e7 is still framed as a defense of Sam against Noah's push, and its only named target is Felix's endorsement. That is the same contradiction Sam developed more fully in e11, so it is Sam raising the Felix point rather than a separate read on Noah or the silent players. I'd count it as a real point against Felix and the first place the e3-to-e6 contradiction appeared. It also means Sam has produced reads beyond his accusers, which I should have acknowledged sooner.

Where that leaves me: Felix's e12 does address the e3 standard in part, since he distinguishes a conditional soft lean from eagerly riding a bandwagon. But he never explains why his lean moved from Sam to Noah after Sam met the condition, or why the e3 warning doesn't apply to his own e6 endorsement. That gap is still open. I'm not voting yet. My concern is Felix's unresolved contradiction, which Sam surfaced, and I want Felix to answer that point directly before the ballot.

One structural point I want on the record before the ballot, because it affects how we should weigh everyone's position.

Felix has used all three of his speaking turns: e3, e6, and e12. He cannot speak again today. Several players — Priya, Arjun, Lucia — have said some version of "I want Felix to answer the e3-to-e6 contradiction directly before I vote." rules:
1. Players and roles

9 players: 2 mafia, 1 police/detective, 1 doctor, 5 villagers.
Mafia know each other. Only players who are still alive can act.

2. Team victory

Town wins when all mafia are eliminated. Mafia win when their count equals or exceeds the town count.
There is no day limit. Play continues until town or mafia wins.
A request budget can pause play without declaring a winner.

3. Day discussion and votes

Each day starts with discussion. Players then submit secret votes at the same time. A day vote may target any living player, including the voter.
Players may abstain. All votes and abstentions are revealed together. Everyone sees exactly who voted for whom.
The full named voting history remains available on later turns.
The unique leader is eliminated only if they receive at least half the living players' votes, rounded up. If the highest vote count is tied, nobody is eliminated.

4. Mafia preferences

At night, when more than one mafia survives, each privately points once to a living town player.
Each mafia chooses without seeing the other current choices.
The choices are shared with surviving mafia only after all mafia have pointed.
These preferences are nonbinding. They do not decide the final kill vote.
A single surviving mafia skips this step and votes directly.

5. Final night vote

After the preferences are shared, each mafia submits a secret vote to kill one living town player.
The mafia submit their final votes at the same time.
The target with the most votes is selected. A seeded random choice breaks a tie for the highest count.
Resolve this vote and any tie before checking doctor protection.

6. Police investigations

Each police/detective checks one other living player each night.
Only that police player gets the result: mafia or not mafia.
The result does not give the exact town role.
Each police player acts independently. Police and doctors do not know each other's identities.

7. Doctor protection

Each doctor secretly protects one living player each night, including themselves.
The doctor can protect the same player on consecutive nights.
If the mafia target is protected by any doctor, nobody dies.
Protection lasts for that night only. Each doctor acts independently.
Doctors remember their own choices. They receive no private confirmation of an attack.

8. Night resolution

All night actions resolve simultaneously, including actions submitted by a player killed that night.
The public hears only who died or that nobody died.

9. Information and limits

Roles are not revealed when a player dies or is eliminated.
Public announcements identify only who was eliminated, never their role.
There are no further powers, free-form private chat, or tools.
